chapters.title: Chapter 3: Reading a Deal as an Investor

lessons.title: Accretion vs Dilution: Does the Deal Add to EPS?

children.text: Almost every acquisition announcement on an Indian earnings call includes one reassuring line: "The transaction will be EPS accretive from the first full year." Analysts nod, the stock steadies, and many investors assume the deal must be good. It is worth knowing exactly what that sentence promises, because a deal can add to earnings per share and still make you poorer, and a deal that dilutes EPS can make you richer.

body.text: EPS accretion is arithmetic, not value creation. A deal adds to EPS when the earnings bought are cheap relative to how the acquirer pays for them. Whether it creates value still depends on synergies versus premium. Use accretion to understand the optics, and use Lesson 1.2's test to judge the deal.

children.text: The Pro Forma EPS Formula
A deal is
accretive
if the combined company's
pro forma EPS
is higher than the acquirer's standalone EPS, and
dilutive
if it is lower.

markDefs.definition: A deal that raises the acquirer's earnings per share compared with what it would have earned without the deal.
Earnings per share calculated as if the deal had already happened, combining both companies' profits and adjusting for funding costs and new shares issued.
A deal that lowers the acquirer's earnings per share compared with what it would have earned without the deal.

body.latex: \text{Pro forma EPS} = \frac{PAT_{\text{acquirer}} + PAT_{\text{target}} + \text{After-tax synergies} - \text{After-tax funding cost}}{\text{Acquirer's shares} + \text{New shares issued}}
body.caption: Funding cost is interest on new debt, or interest income given up on cash spent. New shares appear only when the acquirer pays in stock.

children.text: Worked Example: Konkan Paints Buys Tungabhadra Tiles

Konkan Paints, our fictional acquirer, wants to buy 100% of Tungabhadra Tiles, another fictional listed company, at ₹180 per share, a 20% premium to its market price of ₹150. To keep the maths clean, ignore synergies for now and assume a 25% tax rate.
Option 1: Pay in Konkan shares

Konkan issues new shares at its market price of ₹500. New shares = ₹1,800 crore ÷ ₹500 = 3.6 crore. Pro forma EPS = (₹500 crore + ₹100 crore) ÷ (20 crore + 3.6 crore) = ₹600 crore ÷ 23.6 crore = ₹25.42. That is 1.7% above Konkan's standalone ₹25. Accretive.
Option 2: Pay with cash already on the balance sheet

Konkan's cash earns 7% a year before tax. Spending ₹1,800 crore gives up ₹1,800 crore × 7% × (1 minus 25%) = ₹94.5 crore of after-tax interest income. Pro forma EPS = (₹500 crore + ₹100 crore minus ₹94.5 crore) ÷ 20 crore = ₹505.5 crore ÷ 20 crore = ₹25.28. Accretive by 1.1%.
Option 3: Borrow the money

Konkan borrows ₹1,800 crore at 9%. After-tax interest = ₹1,800 crore × 9% × 75% = ₹121.5 crore. Pro forma EPS = (₹600 crore minus ₹121.5 crore) ÷ 20 crore = ₹478.5 crore ÷ 20 crore = ₹23.93. That is 4.3% below ₹25. Dilutive.

body.title: Konkan Paints EPS: same deal, three ways to pay

body.text: Nothing about Tungabhadra Tiles changed across the three options. Same business, same price, same profits. Only the funding changed, and the EPS verdict flipped from accretive to dilutive. That alone should tell you EPS accretion is a statement about financing arithmetic, not about whether Konkan bought a good business at a good price.

children.text: Shortcuts: Predict the Answer Without the Full Calculation
Before synergies, you can call accretion or dilution by comparing the target's
earnings yield
at the price paid with the after-tax cost of the funding.

markDefs.definition: Earnings per share divided by price per share, or 1 ÷ P/E. At a P/E of 18x, the earnings yield is about 5.56%.

body.caption: Accretion rules of thumb, before synergies

cells: P/E paid is below the acquirer's own P/E
Target's earnings yield at the price paid exceeds after-tax interest income given up
Target's earnings yield at the price paid exceeds after-tax interest cost

body.title: Raise the premium
body.prompt: Tungabhadra's board holds out, and Konkan agrees to pay ₹225 per share, a 50% premium, entirely in Konkan shares at ₹500 each. Ignoring synergies, what is Konkan's pro forma EPS? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Purchase price = ₹225 × 10 crore = ₹2,250 crore. New shares = ₹2,250 crore ÷ ₹500 = 4.5 crore. Pro forma EPS = ₹600 crore ÷ 24.5 crore = ₹24.49, below ₹25, so dilutive. The shortcut agrees: the P/E paid is now ₹225 ÷ ₹10 = 22.5x, above Konkan's 20x.

body.title: Find the break-even price
body.prompt: In an all-stock deal with no synergies, what is the highest price per Tungabhadra share, in rupees, that Konkan can pay without diluting its EPS?
body.explanation: Break-even is when the P/E paid equals Konkan's P/E of 20x. Price = 20 × ₹10 EPS = ₹200. Check: ₹2,000 crore ÷ ₹500 = 4 crore new shares, and ₹600 crore ÷ 24 crore = ₹25, exactly Konkan's standalone EPS.

body.title: The cash deal test
body.textWithBlank: A debt-funded acquisition is accretive before synergies when the target's earnings ___ at the price paid is higher than the after-tax cost of debt.
body.explanation: Earnings yield is the inverse of the P/E paid. If the target earns more per rupee spent than the borrowed rupee costs after tax, EPS rises.

children.text: Why Accretion Can Fool You
The P/E game.

A highly valued acquirer can buy almost any lower-P/E company with its own shares and report accretion, even if it overpays and the target's growth is poor. The market should then assign the combined company a lower P/E to reflect the slower-growing earnings it bought, so EPS rises while the share price does not.
Leverage adds risk.
When cheap debt makes a deal accretive, the higher EPS comes with a riskier balance sheet. Investors typically demand a lower P/E for more debt, which can offset the EPS gain.
Loss-making companies break the maths.

When Zomato bought Blinkit in an all-stock deal in 2022, both businesses were making losses. EPS accretion or dilution tells you nothing useful in that situation. Investors had to judge the deal on strategy, the value of the shares issued and the path to profitability.

columns.label: Accretive but can destroy value
points: A 50x P/E acquirer pays 40x for a slow-growing target in stock
A deal funded with cheap debt just before rates rise
Premium far exceeds realistic synergies, but the target's P/E paid is still below the acquirer's
Reported EPS excludes large amortisation of acquired intangibles

columns.label: Dilutive but can create value
points: Buying a fast-growing business whose profits are small today but compounding
Large cost synergies that take two to three years to arrive
Paying in shares to avoid taking on risky debt
A strategic asset that protects the acquirer's core business from a competitor

body.title: Accretive means good?
body.question: A fictional consumer tech company trading at 60x earnings buys a fictional traditional retailer at 30x earnings, entirely in its own shares. Management calls the deal "strongly EPS accretive" and says synergies are "to be quantified". What can you conclude?
options: The deal creates value because it is strongly accretive
The deal is accretive mainly because the acquirer's P/E is twice the P/E paid, which says nothing about whether it creates value
The deal must be dilutive because 30x is an expensive price for a retailer
Accretion proves the synergies will be large
body.explanation: In an all-stock deal, paying 30x with 60x paper is accretive almost automatically. Whether value is created depends on synergies versus the premium, and management has not even quantified synergies. The market may also re-rate the combined company towards a lower P/E, because a chunk of its earnings now comes from a slower-growing retailer.

body.title: Adjusted EPS, amortisation and the fine print

children.text: Under Ind AS 103, an acquirer records the target's identifiable assets at fair value, including intangibles such as brands, customer relationships and technology. Intangibles with a finite life are amortised, which reduces reported profit for years. Any remaining excess is goodwill, which is not amortised but tested for impairment every year.

Because amortisation drags down reported EPS, companies often present an "adjusted" or "cash" EPS that excludes it. Check which EPS management means when it says "accretive", whether one-time integration costs are excluded, and whether synergies assumed in the calculation are already fully included in year one. Lesson 3.3 looks at what happens when goodwill has to be written down.

body.title: Decode the earnings call
body.scenario: A fictional listed mid-cap, Aravalli Chemicals, trades at 25x earnings. It announces a ₹4,000 crore cash acquisition of a private specialty chemicals firm earning ₹200 crore after tax, funded entirely with new borrowing at 8.5%. On the call, the CFO says the deal will be "EPS accretive in year one on an adjusted basis, including ₹60 crore of run-rate synergies". Assume a 25% tax rate.
body.prompt: Test the CFO's claim. What does the accretion depend on, and what questions would you ask?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Before synergies: earnings yield at the price paid = ₹200 crore ÷ ₹4,000 crore = 5%. After-tax cost of debt = 8.5% × 75% = 6.375%. On those numbers alone, the deal is dilutive: ₹200 crore of profit bought against ₹4,000 crore × 6.375% = ₹255 crore of after-tax interest.
2. The gap is ₹55 crore. The CFO needs the ₹60 crore of synergies, and they must be after tax, to turn it accretive. So accretion depends entirely on synergies arriving in full in year one.
3. Question: are the ₹60 crore of synergies pre-tax or after tax? Pre-tax ₹60 crore is only ₹45 crore after tax, which is not enough to cover the ₹55 crore gap.
4. Question: is ₹60 crore the year one figure or the eventual run-rate? Run-rate synergies usually take two to three years.
5. Question: what does "adjusted" exclude? Amortisation of acquired intangibles and integration costs can be large.
6. Balance sheet: ₹4,000 crore of new debt raises leverage. Check net debt to EBITDA before and after the deal.
7. Value test: separately from EPS, compare the present value of realistic synergies with the premium over the target's standalone value.

body.title: When management says "EPS accretive"
steps: Identify how the deal is paid for: shares, cash on hand or new debt
Compare the P/E paid with the acquirer's P/E, or the earnings yield with the after-tax funding cost
Find out whether synergies are included, and whether they are after tax and for year one
Check whether "adjusted" EPS excludes amortisation or integration costs
Look at leverage after the deal
Separately apply the value test: realistic synergies versus premium paid

body.label: Screener.in
body.description: Pull up the acquirer and any listed target to compare their P/E ratios, profits and share counts, the three inputs you need for a quick accretion check.

cards.definition: A deal that raises the acquirer's EPS above its standalone EPS.
A deal that lowers the acquirer's EPS below its standalone EPS.
Combined profits, adjusted for funding costs and synergies, divided by combined shares after the deal.
Offer price per share divided by the target's EPS.
EPS divided by price, or 1 ÷ P/E.
Before synergies, an all-stock deal is accretive when the P/E paid is below the acquirer's own P/E.
Before synergies, a debt-funded deal is accretive when the target's earnings yield at the price paid exceeds the after-tax cost of debt.

points: Pro forma EPS combines both companies' profits, adds after-tax synergies, subtracts after-tax funding costs and divides by the new share count.
The same deal can be accretive or dilutive depending on funding: Konkan's EPS was ₹25.42 paying in shares, ₹25.28 paying from cash and ₹23.93 borrowing.
All-stock deals are accretive before synergies when the P/E paid is below the acquirer's P/E. Cash deals are accretive when the earnings yield beats the after-tax funding cost.
High-P/E acquirers can report accretion on almost any lower-P/E purchase, which says nothing about value.
Always check whether accretion claims rely on synergies, and whether "adjusted" EPS excludes amortisation or integration costs.
Judge value with the synergies versus premium test, not the EPS headline.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, tax or accounting advice. Konkan Paints, Tungabhadra Tiles, Aravalli Chemicals and the companies in the quiz are fictional. The 25% tax rate is a simplification of the effective corporate tax rate for Indian companies under the concessional regime. Mentioning a real company is not a recommendation to buy or sell its shares.
